Good morning, judges, teachers, students, and families. Welcome to the [Year] High School Science Fair.

Today we gather to celebrate curiosity. Every poster on these tables began with a question someone dared to ask. Some of those questions are simple. Others, like the one I want to talk about, have kept scientists awake for centuries.

Picture the ocean. At the surface, sunlight pours down like a golden waterfall. But below about a thousand meters, the light disappears. It is pitch black, colder, and under crushing pressure. Yet in that darkness, something glows.

Bioluminescence is the ability of living things to produce their own light. Scientists estimate that roughly eighty percent of deep-sea creatures can do it. Fireflies do it on land. Fungi do it in forests. But the deep sea is where the phenomenon becomes truly astonishing.

Why would an animal need light where there is no sun? Some creatures use it as a lure. The anglerfish dangles a glowing bait to attract prey. Others use it as a disguise. The hatchetfish carries a faint glow on its belly so that predators looking up see only the shimmering surface above. Some species flash brilliant patterns to startle enemies or to signal mates across miles of water.

Here is the mystery. Light requires energy, and energy is scarce in the deep. Most deep-sea organisms cannot photosynthesize. So how do they make light without sunlight? The answer lies in chemistry. They combine a molecule called luciferin with an enzyme called luciferase, and the reaction releases light. But the deep-sea versions of these molecules are chemically different from those on land. They evolved independently, again and again, in total isolation.

That repetition is what fascinates me. Evolution found the same solution to the same problem, over and over, in the darkest place on Earth.

[TIP] As you explore your projects today, remember that the best science often begins with wonder rather than answers.

The deep ocean still holds more than half of the planet's life. Every year, new species are discovered, and many of them glow. The next great mystery may be waiting in a jar on one of these tables.

Thank you, and enjoy the fair.

THE PENNY JAR AND THE PASSBOOK

The kitchen smelled of cinnamon and old paper when Maya came home from school. Her grandmother, Ruth, was sitting at the table with a chipped blue jar and a leather-bound book that looked like it had been carried in a pocket for decades.

"Sit," Ruth said, and pulled out a chair. "Today we're learning about money. Not the kind you spend, but the kind that grows."

Maya frowned. "Money doesn't grow on trees."

"True. But it can grow in a jar, if you're patient." Ruth opened the jar. Inside were pennies, stacked in uneven columns, some shiny, some dull with age. "These are the first hundred dollars I ever saved. I was your age, and I wanted a bicycle. I couldn't afford it, so I put every spare penny in this jar."

She flipped open the passbook. The pages were yellowed, and the handwriting was careful, almost military.

"Every month, I wrote down how much I had," Ruth said. "And every year, the bank added a little interest. That's the magic part. Interest is money paid to you for letting them use your money. Then next year, they pay interest on the interest too. That's called compound interest. It's like a snowball rolling downhill. At first it's small, but it keeps getting bigger."

Maya leaned closer. "So the pennies keep making pennies?"

"Sort of. The bank does the work. But the idea is the same. Money that sits still can start working for you."

Ruth pointed to a line in the book. "Look here. After ten years, I had more than I put in. After twenty, even more. I never touched it. I just kept adding pennies."

Maya counted the pennies in the jar. "That's a lot."

"More than I expected," Ruth admitted. "I thought I'd need a bicycle. I got a house instead."

She closed the passbook and set it beside the jar. "Your turn. Put a dollar in every week. Don't spend it. Don't even look at it. In five years, you'll have more than fifty dollars. In twenty, you'll have something real."

Maya hesitated. "What if I want to buy something?"

"Then you'll learn to wait," Ruth said gently. "Patience is the hardest part. The money grows while you sleep."

That night, Maya tucked a dollar into the jar. It felt small, but it felt like the beginning of something.

Johann Sebastian Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier, published in two volumes in 1722 and 1742, stands as one of the most important landmarks in keyboard music. Its significance lies in how it reshaped the way composers thought about harmony, structure, and the instrument itself.

Before Bach, many keyboard works favored a few familiar keys. The tuning systems of the day made distant keys sound harsh, so composers often avoided them. Bach changed that by writing a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key. This bold plan showed that music could travel freely across the entire chromatic spectrum.

The result is a collection of pieces that are both deeply expressive and rigorously logical. Each fugue explores a single theme through imitation, inversion, and stretto, while each prelude offers a mood ranging from gentle to stormy. Together, they form a kind of musical encyclopedia, a balloon of ideas that lifts listeners into new realms of sound.

Bach also treated the keyboard as a complete instrument, not merely a tool for accompanying singers. His writing demands clarity, balance, and careful attention to every note. In doing so, he helped establish the keyboard as a solo voice capable of carrying an entire argument.

Later composers, from Beethoven to Debussy, drew on this foundation. The Well-Tempered Clavier remains a model of how imagination and discipline can work together, a lesson that still resonates today.

Handel and Haydn both wrote music that still sounds fresh today, yet their styles reveal how musical taste changed between the Baroque and Classical eras. Handel's Messiah, finished in 1741, belongs to the Baroque world. Its choruses are bold, its melodies sweep across the page, and its orchestra often doubles the voices. Haydn's symphonies, by contrast, favor clarity and balance. His melodies are simple and memorable, his rhythms steady, and his orchestration lets each instrument speak in its own voice. Both composers loved the human voice, but Handel used it for drama, while Haydn used it for charm.

******

If you listen closely, Handel and Haydn sound like two neighbors with different personalities. Handel's music is full of ornamentation, sudden shifts, and emotional intensity. In Messiah, the chorus "Hallelujah" builds to a thunderous climax that feels almost overwhelming. Haydn's music, however, is more relaxed and playful. His symphonies often surprise listeners with a quiet passage that suddenly bursts into a lively tune. Both composers wrote for choirs and orchestras, yet Handel favored grand gestures, while Haydn favored wit. Together, they show how music moved from the elaborate to the elegant.

Fats are a major part of every meal, yet not all of them behave the same way in our bodies. The key difference lies in how their molecules are built.

Saturated fats pack tightly together because their carbon chains hold no double bonds. They are solid at room temperature, like butter, lard, and coconut oil. Eating too much can raise LDL cholesterol, which may contribute to heart disease.

Unsaturated fats contain one or more double bonds, which create kinks that keep the molecules loose. Olive oil, avocado, nuts, and fish are rich in these fats. Research links them to better heart health and lower inflammation.

Trans fats are the most harmful. They form when manufacturers add hydrogen to liquid oils, a process called hydrogenation. The result is a fat that is both solid and chemically unstable. It raises bad cholesterol while lowering good cholesterol. Many countries have banned it, but it still hides in some baked goods and fried snacks.

The distinction matters because small daily choices add up. Swapping butter for olive oil, choosing whole fish over processed meat, and reading labels for partially hydrogenated oils can lower long-term health risks. A balanced plate, with plenty of unsaturated fats and little trans fat, is a simple way to eat well.

The ketogenic diet places cyclists in a state of fat adaptation, where the body relies heavily on fatty acids and ketones for fuel. However, the trade-off is a slower pace at moderate intensities, since fat oxidation cannot match the speed of carbohydrate burning. After a long ride, many cyclists feel hungrier and more irritable, and some experience headaches or low mood. These symptoms usually fade as the body adapts, but they can make the early transition uncomfortable.

Overall, the ketogenic diet can work well for steady, long-distance riding, but it may limit performance on hilly or fast sections. Macronutrients are the nutrients your body needs in large amounts to grow, move, and stay healthy. There are three: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

**Carbohydrates**
- Your body's main source of energy.
- Found in bread, rice, pasta, fruits, and vegetables.

**Proteins**
- Build and repair muscles, skin, and organs.
- Found in meat, eggs, beans, nuts, and dairy.
- Your body can't store protein, so you need it every day.

**Fats**
- Provide long-lasting energy and help your body absorb vitamins.
- Found in oils, nuts, avocados, and fatty fish.
- Not all fats are equal. Saturated fats (like butter) should be eaten in moderation, while unsaturated fats (like olive oil) are healthier.

- Balance matters more than counting calories.

The early nineteenth century saw the rise of the public concert hall as a central institution for music consumption, and it reshaped how composers earned a living. Before this era, most composers depended on court or church patronage, but the expanding middle class now paid to hear new works performed. This shift turned composers into entrepreneurs who had to market their own music to audiences rather than waiting for aristocratic commissions.

Publishing grew alongside the concert culture, as sheet music became a profitable commodity sold to amateur musicians and aspiring professionals. Publishers began commissioning works, promoting composers, and building reputations through catalogues and advertisements, which gave creators a new source of income. However, composers often received only a small share of the profits, since publishers controlled printing, distribution, and sales.

The relationship between performance and publication also created new risks, because a work that failed at the box office could still sell well as sheet music. Conversely, a popular piece could be pirated or out of print, leaving composers vulnerable to market fluctuations beyond their control. These tensions laid the groundwork for later debates over copyright, royalties, and the modern music industry.

The short version: added sugars hide in plain sight, so read the label like a detective.

4. **Beware of "reduced" claims.** "Reduced sugar" only means at least 25 percent less than the original product, which may still be high.

5. **Look at serving size.** A "healthy" serving of 1/2 cup can add up quickly if you eat two.

6. **Compare similar products.** Put a few brands side by side on the shelf to see which has the least added sugar.

7. **Watch for sweetened versions.** Yogurt, granola, bread, and sauces often have added sugar. Choose plain or unsweetened versions and add your own fruit or honey.

8. **Check the front of the package.** Many brands use "sugar-free" or "no sugar added" badges to distract you. Always confirm with the label.

9. **Remember the daily limit.** The FDA suggests keeping added sugars under 10 percent of your daily calories, roughly 25 grams for most adults.

10. **Trust your gut.** If a product tastes sweet but the label says otherwise, it probably has hidden sugar.

Congratulations! It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed. Here are the key nutrients that matter most, and why each one matters:

**Folic acid (folate)**
Folic acid helps build your baby's brain and spinal cord. Taking it before conception and during the first weeks of pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects. Aim for 400–800 micrograms daily, usually through a prenatal vitamin.

**Iron**
Your blood volume grows significantly during pregnancy, and iron carries oxygen to your baby. Low iron can cause anemia, which may lead to fatigue and complications. Many women need 27 mg daily, often with vitamin C to improve absorption.

**Calcium**
Calcium builds your baby's bones and teeth. If your diet doesn't supply enough, your body draws calcium from your own bones, so it's important to keep yours strong. Aim for about 1,000 mg daily.

**Vitamin D**
Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and supports your baby's bone development. It also supports your immune system. Many people need a supplement, especially if they get little sun exposure.

**Iodine**
Iodine is essential for your baby's brain and thyroid development. The recommended amount is 220 micrograms daily.

**DHA (an omega-3 fatty acid)**
DHA supports your baby's brain and eye development. Many prenatal vitamins include it, or you can eat fatty fish like salmon, keeping mercury intake low.

**Choline**
Choline supports your baby's brain development and helps prevent neural tube defects. Aim for 450 mg daily, found in eggs, meat, and dairy.

**Protein**
Protein builds your baby's tissues and supports your own body's changes. Aim for about 71 grams daily.

**Tips**
- A good prenatal vitamin covers most of these needs.
- Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein.
- Avoid alcohol, limit caffeine, and avoid high-mercury fish.
- Talk with your healthcare provider about your specific needs, since every pregnancy is different.

- **Animal sources:** Eggs, chicken, beef, fish, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, and milk. These are complete proteins, meaning they contain all the amino acids your body needs.
- **Plant sources:** Lentils, beans, tofu, tempeh, edamame, quinoa, and nuts. Combine different plant proteins across the day to cover your needs.
- **Supplements:** Whey protein is convenient, but it's not necessary. Whole food usually works just as well.

**A simple way to track it:**

Think of protein as your **compass** for building muscle. It points you in the right direction, but it won't carry you there on its own.

Don't treat protein as a **ticket** to results. You also need resistance training, enough calories, and sleep.

**Practical tip:** If you're eating three meals a day, try to include a protein source at each one. A boiled egg, a scoop of Greek yogurt, or a handful of lentils can be enough.

**Bottom line:** For most beginners, 70–100 grams of protein daily is plenty. If you're very active or trying to gain muscle, go toward 100–120 grams.

And remember: consistency is the **candle** that keeps your progress burning. Small, steady habits beat perfection every time.
